title: Overdubbed telephoned parts versus live sessions
summary: He objects to dead recordings made without interaction.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: We did those things at Bob Festein's studio and Bob (inaudible), which
they don't do anymore. Now everybody telephones his part, which is a terrible thing. It drives me insane. It makes for a lifeless recording.
People all used to wonder how they could do it the most are the rhythm section players who have to come in and just lay down a basic track without anything having been done before.
To anybody's. It's there but it doesn't live; it's dead.
It's done, obviously, but it is obviously very difficult for say a drummer to play a kick to a band that isn't there.
Well it depends on how well the drum parts are.
Yes, but he's not reacting to the people around him. It's nothing.
No, it's a very sterile process.
It comes out sounding very neat, because they can handle it, but it's dead. I find I can't listen over and over again to a record made like that either; one time through and that's it.
